entities.name: Anglican Communion
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Anglican Communion, formally constituted in 1867 at the first Lambeth Conference convened by Archbishop Longley, is a worldwide fellowship of 42 member churches and 85 million Christians — the third-largest Christian denomination — bound by common heritage from the Church of England but governed independently in each member country. The Communion's 'instruments of communion' (Lambeth Conference, Primates Meeting, Archbishop of Canterbury, Anglican Consultative Council) attempt to coordinate an increasingly diverse fellowship across 165 countries without central authority.

Anglicanisms' global spread followed British colonialism: the Church of England's colonial chaplains established parishes in North America (1607), India (1813), Australia (1788), New Zealand (1814), Africa (1804), and the Caribbean — creating local churches that became autonomous. The Episcopal Church USA (founded 1789) was the first to achieve independence. Post-colonial Anglican churches in Africa (Uganda, Nigeria, Kenya, South Africa) now contain the majority of global Anglicans and have become more conservative than their North American and European counterparts.

The Windsor Report (2004) and subsequent crises over LGBTQ+ inclusion have created a deep north-south divide in the Communion. The election of Gene Robinson as first openly gay bishop (New Hampshire, 2003) prompted Global South African and Asian provinces to suspend communion with the Episcopal Church. The 2022 Global Anglican Future Conference (GAFCON) in Rwanda — attended by 1,300 delegates representing 85% of global Anglicanism — effectively constituted a parallel Anglican body, making the Communion's structural future uncertain.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Anglican Communion's 2022 GAFCON crisis — with 85% of global Anglicanism effectively seceding from the liberal western churches over LGBTQ+ inclusion — is the largest Protestant schism of the 21st century and the most significant consequence of British colonial Christianization.
